synopsis: The biography traces J. Edgar Hoover from his Washington upbringing through nearly five decades directing the FBI under eight presidents. It examines how he modernized federal law enforcement while using surveillance, secrecy, publicity, and political alliances to accumulate personal power, police dissent, enforce racial hierarchies, and shape twentieth-century American conservatism.

This biography follows Walter Lippmann from his Progressive-era beginnings at Harvard and The New Republic through six decades as a journalist, policy adviser, and public intellectual. It places his evolving ideas about democracy, public opinion, war, and American power alongside the two world wars, the Depression, the Cold War, Vietnam, and the rise and erosion of the American Century.

sources.title: Walter Lippmann and the American Century

synopsis: The fourth volume of the Lyndon Johnson biography covers 1958 through 1964, from his failed presidential bid and constricted vice presidency to the assassination of John F. Kennedy. It traces how Johnson took command of a grieving administration and used his legislative skill to move civil rights measures and the War on Poverty through Congress.

The book examines Japanese life under the Allied occupation from surrender in 1945 through 1952, including defeat, deprivation, black markets, censorship, political reform, and cultural upheaval. It analyzes the unequal relationship between occupier and occupied, the treatment of Emperor Hirohito and war responsibility, and the contradictory experiences of humiliation, democratization, and liberation from militarism.

This biography traces Frederick Douglass from enslavement and escape through his rise as an abolitionist orator, editor, writer, political thinker, and diplomat. It connects his public campaigns for emancipation, Reconstruction, voting rights, and equality with his evolving ideas, family responsibilities, personal relationships, and efforts to interpret freedom in the decades after slavery.

Surveying a thousand years of technological history, the book argues that progress is fragile rather than inevitable and explains why leading societies repeatedly lose their innovative edge. It contrasts decentralized systems that encourage experimentation with bureaucratic institutions that efficiently scale existing technologies, showing how failure to shift between them can produce stagnation in economies from Song China to the modern United States and China.

The book reconstructs Nazi Germany’s economy to explain how resource constraints, rearmament, racial conquest, forced labor, and mass murder became intertwined. It argues that Hitler pursued war to build a continental empire capable of competing with the United States, even though Germany lacked the food, fuel, industrial capacity, and strategic means needed for that struggle.

The book examines why roughly one billion people in a group of poor countries remained outside the gains of global growth. It identifies four recurring traps—armed conflict, dependence on natural resources, landlocked geography with weak neighbors, and bad governance—and evaluates aid, trade preferences, legal standards, security intervention, and other policies intended to help countries escape them.

The book investigates ExxonMobil’s operations, internal culture, and political influence from the 1989 Exxon Valdez spill through the early twenty-first century. It follows the company’s dealings with governments, oil-producing states, communities, and regulators to show how a highly centralized corporation manages geopolitical risk, climate science, lobbying, security, and the pursuit of new reserves.
